list.listitem: Avoid unnecessary use of medications that may cause cutaneous drug reaction, especially antibiotics. C
Make the diagnosis based on history and physical examination. C
Avoid repeat exposures for patients with Type 1 reactions or Stevens Johnson syndrome. C

For Type 1 (anaphylactic) allergic reactions, stabilize patient, give parenteral epinephrine if anaphylaxis or respiratory distress; first-generation histamine blockers; and IV steroids followed by oral steroids. C

Due to an incorrect initial diagnosis or waning immunity, many patients reporting a remote history of penicillin allergy may be able to tolerate a penicillin. Due to different side chains, penicillin allergic patients should not have cross reactivity to third and fourth generation cephalosporins. C

background.definition: A cutaneous drug reaction is an unwanted response to a drug. The drug may be administered topically or systemically and result in the reaction.

list.listitem: Ten to 80 per 1000, which varies by medication exposure. Antibiotics tend to have among the highest rates of cutaneous drug reactions, followed by anti-inflammatories, analgesics, and antipyretics.

SSRIs may be responsible for cutaneous drug reactions.The most common psychotropic drugs implicated in DRESS (Drug Eruption with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) are carbamezapine, lamotigine, phenytoin, valproate and phenobarbital.DRESS presents 1 to 2 months after initiation of new medication.
Children are more likely to get a serum sickness reaction than adults.
Adverse drug reactions account for 4.1% of hospital admissions in general and 16.6% of admissions in the elderly (data not confined to cutaneous reactions).
Drug eruptions account for 25-30% of adverse drug events.

In a prospective trial of hospitalized patients with a cutaneous drug reaction, the highest rates of associated underlying disorders were HIV positive patients (19%), hepatitis (12%), and connective tissue disease (10%).
See for the most common causes of cutaneous drug reactions.

A study found that the following factors were associated with an increased likelihood of adverse drug events in hospitalized patients: comorbidities, recent antibiotic use, changes in medications, age >80 years, recent hospital admission, renal failure, arrival by ambulance, and using 3 or more medications.

There are multiple etiologies for cutaneous drug reactions, including allergic (immunologic), pseudo-allergic, toxic, and ligand-induced apoptosis. Allergic reactions with cutaneous findings are classified as Type 1 to Type 4.

Type 1 IgE-mediated reactions with hives and possible anaphylaxis. These require prior sensitization to form IgE antibodies, leading to anaphylactic reactions upon reexposure to the offending medication.
Type 2 reactions do not typically cause cutaneous findings, but are responsible for hemolytic reactions.
Type 3 reactions are due to complement fixation and immune complex deposition in the skin. This can cause morbilliform or expanding annular rash, the "serum sickness" reaction.
Type 4 reactions are due to a cell-mediated immune response seen in contact dermatitis or a positive PPD.
Pseudoallergic reactions are because of the nonallergic release of histamine by X-ray contrast dyes or vancomycin.
Toxic reactions (e.g., to ampicillin) are not clearly understood, but are morbilliform and seen in 9% of patients and 90% of patients with mononucleosis.
Fas ligand-induced apoptosis occurs when an offending drug induces death of keratinocytes and causes Stevens Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Reactions to tumor necrosis factor alpha inhibitors are common. Certain drug reactions (for example, to carbamazepine) are associated with HLA antigens.
Angioedema is caused by a variety of mechnisms, see .
Take a careful history with attention to medication use. C
Examine skin and mucous membranes and make diagnosis clinically. C
Consider over-the-counter and herbal supplements in history. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Adverse reaction to food or other substance
DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms), also known as DIHS (Drug-Induced Hypersensitivity Syndrome)
Differential.Differential_Features: Measles-like eruption with eosinophilia and organ involvement
Diffuse erythema with areas of denuded, necrotic epidermis, with mucosal involvement
Localized erythema or vesicle in identical location when challenged with the same medication

list.listitem: Suspect cutaneous drug reaction in patients presenting with a rash or localized skin findings, and recent addition of one or more medications.

Carefully review all medications including over-the-counter medications, herbal preparations, and supplements with attention to any recent additions. Antibiotics and anticonvulsants are among the most common medications leading to cutaneous drug reactions (see ). Query the patient about previous reactions or exposures to the same medications for possible sensitization.
Only 21% of children with a cutaneous drug eruption have a positive family history.

Review the vital signs for tachycardia, hypotension, or tachypnea. Listen to the lungs for wheezes. Examine the mucous membranes for sloughing, exudates, swelling, or exanthems. See for typical skin findings.

Unless presenting with severe illness, routine testing is not indicated since diagnosis is based on history and physical examination. Rechallenging with the offending agent may confirm an allergy, but the risks must be weighed against the benefits.
Skin patch testing is positive in 21.3% of children with suspected allergic rash, but only 2.3% had a repeat reaction on rechallenge.
Complement levels decrease in anaphylactic reactions, while serum IgE levels may be increased in sensitized patients.
Tryptase levels increase with mast cell degranulation.
Skin biopsy can further delineate the skin process if in doubt, but is seldom necessary.

A sensitive (but not very specific) clinical decision rule has been developed to identify patients at risk for adverse drug events. While it can identify over 90% of these patients, it would require a full medication review by a pharmacist in 28% to 41% of patients.

PEN-FAST rule appears to accurately identify adults with low-risk penicillin allergy without the need for allergy testing. For patients who report a PENicillin allergy, presence of F (five years or less since the reaction), A (anaphylaxis or angioedema), S (severe cutaneous reaction), or T (treatment required for reaction) can help stratify patients based on likelihood of a positive allergy test (ie, skin prick, intradermal, or patch test). F is assigned 2 points, A or S 2 points, and T 1 point. Score of 0 represented a likelihood of a positive allergy test of <1%, whereas a score of 1 or 2 had a 5% likelihood of a positive test. Based on the validation of 3 cohorts, the sensitivity was between 70.4% (prevalence 27%) and 87.5% (prevalence 14.4%).

The PEN-FAST score is not useful in children 12 years and younger, with a sensitivity and specificity of 57.0% and 45.7%, respectively, using a cut-off score of 3. Additional study is needed for ages 13-18.

The SULF-FAST risk stratification tool (using the same questions used for PEN-FAST has been validated in a small study (N=125) evaluating patients with reported sulfonamide allergy that were given an oral provocation test. The tool appears to accurately identify (96%) patients that are low risk (SULF-FAST score <3) for whom removable of sulfa allergy was accomplished. The 4% of low risk patients who developed an adverse event only had mild reactions (i.e., skin rash, joint pain, transient fever) that necessitated use of an oral antihistamine and/or ibuprofen/acetaminophen.
Suspect cutaneous drug reaction in patients presenting with a rash and a recent addition of a medication.
Laboratory tests and studies are usually not required, unless a Severe Cutaneous Drug Reaction (SCAR) is suspected.
Immediately discontinue suspected causative medications in severe illness. C
Perform critical and supportive care as needed for associated respiratory or vascular compromise. C
Consider antihistamines, steroids, and epinephrine for stabilization and respiratory distress if needed. C
Stop any potential medications that may be the cause, if possible, and advise the patient to avoid offending medications in the future.

For Type 1 (anaphylactic) allergic reactions: stabilize airway, blood pressure. Administer parenteral epinephrine if anaphylaxis or respiratory distress, and first-generation histamine blockers to block further histamine release. Give IV steroids followed by oral steroids; while steroids are widely recommended and probably beneficial, RCTs are lacking.
Pseudoallergic (histamine release): premedicate with antihistamine and IV steroid if medication unavoidable. For vancomycin, slowing the infusion may be adequate to prevent a reaction.

Stevens Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis: supportive care including intensive care or burn unit to manage skin loss, fluid shifts, and mucous membrane scarring and ocular complications. No evidence to support the use of steroids or immunoglobulins; thalidomide increases mortality. Recent studies indicate possible mortality reduction and decrease length of hospitalization with use of the TNF Alpha inhibitor etanercept.
Ninety seven percent of patients with amino-penicillin reactions can tolerate cefpodoxime or cefixime.

0.6% of patients with self-reported penicillin allergy, and 3% of patients with confirmed penicillin allergy, were also allergic to cefazolin in a meta-analysis. 3.7-4.4% of patients with confirmed cefazolin allergy were also penicillin-allergic.
Admit, treat, and observe any unstable patient and toxic epidermal necrolysis patients (Steven Johnson syndrome).
Supportive care including intensive care or burn unit to manage skin loss, fluid shifts, and mucous membrane scarring and ocular complications.
Death from Type 1 reactions is uncommon but possible; there were 6 nonfood or vaccine-related anaphylactic deaths recorded in Australia from 1997 to 2004. A
Toxic epidermal necrolysis has a 30% mortality rate. A
DRESS (Drug Eruption with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) has estimated mortality rate of 10 to 20% and can result in severe systemic disease as well as reactivation of CMV. B
Most reactions resolve spontaneously with time and removal of causative medication. C
Ninety-seven percent of patients with amino-penicillin reactions can tolerate cefpodoxime or cefixime. B
Exanthems related to illness are very common in children. Often these children will concurrently be taking medication, commonly antibiotics, confounding the cause of the exanthem.
Skin patch testing will be positive in 21.3% of children with suspected allergic rash, but only 2.3% will have a reaction on rechallenge.

Most common and nonspecific: maculopapular diffuse rash seen with toxic ampicillin rash and many other medications
Associated with ill-appearing patient in pustular allergic reaction (Also called AGEP-Acute Generalized Exanthematous Pustulosis)
Serpigenous or coalescing: serum sickness reaction
In fixed drug eruption with associated hyperpigmentation if recurrent
Coumarin reaction of necrosis because of hypercoagulable state
